extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics interested in foliage and landscape technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for painting and judging foliage in landscape work, addressing composition, detail, color, light, and the handling of distance and bough-structure. Emphasizes how to render truth in foliage and how to judge artists' success or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect unity in nature's foliage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature secures an exceeding harmony and repose; her minuteness of parts becomes, at a little distance, one united veil or cloud of leaves, and destroying the evenness of this veil is perhaps a greater fault than destroying its transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend intricate parts into a cloud-like harmony of shade; employ flatness, misty unison, and unity of tone so the eye is kept in perfect repose amid profusion. Display particular beauty across quiet, dim passages of rest rather than by isolated detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-rendering detail / painting leaf by leaf
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters who render every leaf lose the truth of detail and fail at distance: 'They can paint oak leafage faithfully, but do not know where to stop... they are reduced to paint their bushes with dots and touches expressive of leaves three feet broad each.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know where to stop—think in masses for distance. Do not attempt to render leaves separately where it is impossible to see them; maintain simplicity, mass, and obscurity where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine intricacy with unbroken repose (Turner standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal foliage combines 'perfect and ceaseless intricacy' with 'perfect and unbroken repose'—intricacy that nevertheless reads as a unified, restful mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for admirably drawn stems and boundless, transparent intricacy coupled with misty depth; avoid mechanical repetition of a single touch or shell patterns. Use Turner's Marly group as an exemplar: complexity subordinated to unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not paint nearest leaves as finite particulars (Claude's failing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing every particular leaf in the foreground makes nature finite and false: nearest leafage lacking shadows, sparkling lights, and confused intersections is 'more like an ornamental pattern for dress than the painting of a foreground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure nearest leaves have form-modifying shadows, sparkling highlights, and overlapping intersections; avoid repetitive identical leaf-shapes against a flat ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-distance foliage as model of good drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Claude's foliage in the middle distances is 'the finest and truest part of his pictures' and affords 'the best example of good drawing to be found in ancient art,' despite faults in color and stems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study middle distances for correct drawing of mass, flexibility, and intricate but graceful arrangement; be aware of and correct for common faults like false color and insufficiently embedded boughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal termination of trees in symmetrical curves
rubrics_metrics.description: In finely grown trees, bough extremities describe a symmetrical curve (constant for each species); each bough reaches but does not pass this terminal line, filling the curve without break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and indicate the overall silhouette/terminal curve of a tree species when composing; avoid errant boughs that interrupt the symmetry—paint trees as domes or pear-shaped masses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to natural terminal line in composition (Turner's practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turner 'rigidly and constantly' adheres to the principle of terminal curves, arranging abundant complexity under simpler and grander forms than other artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even amid abundant complexity, arrange sprays and branches so they terminate at the assigned limit and collectively suggest the species' ideal silhouette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance finish and sketchiness; avoid over-brilliancy of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: An over-fondness for brilliant execution leads to hasty, sketchlike foliage that lacks the higher virtues and impressiveness of well-finished work: 'Harding's foliage is never sufficiently finished, and has at its best the look of a rapid sketch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow parts to be sketched, but know when patient finish is necessary to render higher virtues. Avoid using a few bold touches to substitute for careful study where finish would reveal truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bough-drawing must follow the unbroken tendency of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The flow of the bough should not be sacrificed to texture; the pencil should follow the grand and unbroken tendency of growth rather than hesitating at dots, stripes, and knots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer composed groups of line and the continuous sweep of growth over textural minutiae. Study branches patiently so individual sprays are convincing without slavishly copying every fragment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose mature and symmetric tree-forms; avoid imperfect leaning forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of tree forms affects truth: choosing imperfect, leaning, or laterally unequal forms yields picturesque but rarely grand or true trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and select well-formed, mature exemplars to attain dignity and character; patient study is required to perceive necessary symmetries and proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceive sketches in shade and color before texture
rubrics_metrics.description: A great sketch is 'conceived entirely in shade and color' with masses blocked out with reference to both; inferior draughtsmen check at textures and petty characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pupils to see where things are light and where they are dark, and draw accordingly; use value blocking to substitute for symbolism and to later add texture only when appropriate (Rembrandt example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crude, scattered, and petty chiaroscuro
rubrics_metrics.description: Crude chiaroscuro—black shadows under distant trees, white highlights on foreground rocks—divides foliage and trunks into separate masses and destroys soft roundings and grand relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek judicious moderation of lights and darks so masses remain coherent; avoid violent oppositions that break the unity of foliage and landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and technical skill are prerequisites for true manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither 'grandeur of manner nor truth of system can atone for the want of knowledge and skill.' Manner without accurate drawing or observation leaves works destitute of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate accurate drawing and thorough knowledge of natural forms; strong manner should rest upon, not replace, demonstrable truth and technical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color must express light rather than be mere local color
rubrics_metrics.description: Local color rendered without correct relation to light and shadow results in 'green paint instead of green light' or misleading darks (e.g., Creswick's equal dark purple on different surfaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render color as affected by sunshine and shadow—use scientific relations of shadow and light so color conveys illumination. Study how sunlight transforms local color rather than copying pigment alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study small portions thoroughly to inform larger effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to draw small portions (boughs, stones) thoroughly undermines larger compositions even when the artist studies large views on the spot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine broad studies with patient close observation of details; small studies refine understanding of form and color needed to unify large-scale works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and over-execution; preserve simplicity and specific character
rubrics_metrics.description: Foliage may be 'remarkable for its intricacy and elegance' yet be affected and always evidently composed in the study; execution can be rough, woolly, or lacking in specific character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for simplicity, sharpness, freshness, and species-specific character. Excessive mannered touches or showy execution diminish truth of foliage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper reverence and fidelity with necessary generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists of reverence and patience (e.g., Linnell, Palmer) may overfill detail or lack discovery of 'what is necessary and unnecessary'—resulting in works where best qualities are hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve careful fidelity while learning what to omit or simplify for clarity and compositional strength; a little selective sharpening or moderation of touch can reveal sterling qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render stems and boughs convincingly among foliage
rubrics_metrics.description: True foliage painting includes well-drawn stems and boughs—not 'claws or serpents'—so that stems sit naturally among leaves and contribute to perceived depth and realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure stems are embedded and related to leaf masses; stems should not look unnaturally nearer than the foliage nor be insufficient among leafage (contrast Claude's faults vs Turner's strengths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe diminishing detail with distance (vaporescence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail and minuteness should diminish with distance so the eye perceives a 'vaporescence'—a flat, misty unison of parts—rather than a repetition of close detail at all depths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ softened edges, reduced contrasts, and unified tone for distant foliage. Reserve crisp detail for where the eye can genuinely perceive it and use misty depth to imply complexity at a distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined truths rest upon demonstrable fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: High, refined artistic truth is often too delicate for verbal proof; however, the coarser demonstrable matters (those that can be explained) are fundamental and must be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master and correct broad, explicable principles (mass, light, proportion, diminishing detail) first; only then can the subtler, nearly ineffable refinements be reliably pursued.
